newsitem.title: TURKEY: Iraqi Kurdish warlord set for tough U.S. talks.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurdish warlord set for tough U.S. talks.

text.p: Baghdad-backed Iraqi Kurdish strongman Massoud Barzani arrived in Turkey on Wednesday for his first talks with U.S. officials since he conquered northern Iraq, effectively ending U.S. operations there.
Washington was expected to try to dissuade Barzani from further cooperation with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein in a bid to pick up the pieces of its shattered policy on north Iraq.
Witnesses said the Kurdish leader was driven through the Habur border crossing in a black Mercedes car accompanied by half a dozen vehicles carrying guards and aides.
A Turkish military helicopter shadowed the convoy as it headed for the southeastern city of Diyarbakir.

Talks are scheduled in the Turkish capital Ankara, later in the day or on Thursday, between Barzani and Robert Pelletreau, U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, U.S. embassy officials said. Barzani will also meet Turkish officials.

Washington has lost influence in northern Iraq since Barzani's forces joined with Iraqi troops and tanks to capture the Kurdish city of Arbil from rival militiaman Jalal Talabani last month, prompting U.S. missile strikes on Iraq.

The U.S. envoy will "repeat the advice privately that we have tried to give Mr. Barzani and Mr. Talabani in public... that Mr. Barzani's relationship with Saddam Hussein cannot be in the long term interest of his people or himself," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday.
Baghdad's involvement in the Kurdish infighting has raised questions on the future of a U.S.-led no-fly zone over northern Iraq, set up in 1991 to protect the Kurds from any Iraqi attack.
The United States helped more than 2,000 pro-U.S. Kurds flee northern Iraq in fear of Saddam last weekend in acknowledgement that Washington had lost much of its leverage in the region.
Fresh fighting between Barzani's forces and Talabani's rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan broke out last month, ending a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that had held for more than a year.
Barzani's group, which blames Washington for not doing enough to halt the Kurdish feud, promised tough talk.
"The KDP leadership will present its case and explain the situation in a frank and direct way," it said in a statement.

The KDP says it was forced to ask Saddam for help because the West did nothing to halt alleged Iranian backing for its rival. "(We believe) the forthcoming talks will clear the confusion in the Kurdish region of Iraq," the KDP said.
State Department spokesman Burns said Washington would try to get the two Kurdish groups to put aside decades of animosity.
"Our objective is to have Mr. Barzani and Mr. Talabani agree to talk about their differences peacefully and across from one another at the negotiating table," he said.
Barzani was also expected to meet Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller for talks on tightening security on their common border, a KDP official said.

Turkey says instability in northern Iraq plays into the hands of its own separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which maintains bases there, but Ankara has yet to unveil details of a proposed security zone in northern Iraq.
